opus-5.5.text:
I think the core idea is quite elegant. Theorem proving has a data scarcity problem: there just aren't that many formalized statements in Lean, and once a prover has learned what it can from them, you hit a wall. STP's answer is to have the model play two roles. One is a conjecturer that proposes new statements, and the other is a prover that tries to prove them. They train each other.

The interesting part is how they decide whether a conjecture is "good." Their main signal is difficulty relative to the current prover. If the prover solves a conjecture every time, it's too easy and teaches nothing. If it never solves it, you have no proof to learn from, and the statement might even be false or ill-posed. So they favor conjectures in the sweet spot, where the prover succeeds only a small fraction of the time. That's essentially curriculum learning that emerges on its own, and I think it's the right intuition. It mirrors how human mathematicians grow: you work on problems just at the edge of what you can do.

There are also some heuristics to keep the conjecturer from gaming the system. For example, they filter out statements that are artificially long or degenerate, and they try to keep the distribution close to real math so it doesn't drift into strange corners of Lean that happen to be hard but are mathematically meaningless.

That said, I see limitations. Difficulty for this particular prover is not the same as mathematical value. A conjecture can be hard because of awkward formalization rather than deep content. The deeper question is how to judge whether a conjecture is *interesting*: whether it connects ideas, generalizes something, or opens up new directions. Human mathematicians have taste for that, and it's very hard to turn into a reward signal. Pass rate is a clean, scalable proxy, which is why it works well for an engineering result, but it doesn't really capture taste.

So my overall view is that it's an important step. It shows that self-play can push past the limits of static datasets in formal math. But if we want AI that does real mathematical discovery, and not just gets better at benchmarks like miniF2F or ProofNet, we'll need richer ways to evaluate conjectures. That might mean measuring usefulness, such as whether proving a conjecture helps prove other things downstream, or building some model of mathematical significance. To me that's one of the most exciting open problems in the field.

r001.rationale: The response contrasts pass rate as a clean, scalable signal with the difficulty of rewarding mathematical taste or interestingness, conveying that conjecture quality lacks an equally clear reward signal.

r002.rationale: It explicitly says difficulty for the prover is not the same as mathematical value and that pass rate does not capture whether a conjecture is interesting.

r003.rationale: The response discusses difficulty and filters for long or degenerate statements, but does not assess relative statement and proof length as a measure of elegance.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the Self-play Theorem Prover paper is one of the more interesting attempts to break out of the data bottleneck that everyone in formal math has been hitting. The basic observation is right: if you only train on existing Lean theorems, you run out of hard, useful problems very quickly. Mathlib is finite, the competition datasets are finite, and once a model has seen them, there's not much signal left. So the idea of having the model play two roles, a conjecturer that proposes new statements and a prover that tries to prove them, is a genuinely good way to manufacture a curriculum on the fly.

Where I'd be a bit more careful is on how they decide which conjectures are worth keeping. The filter is essentially: is this statement provable, is it not trivially provable, and is it roughly at the frontier of what the prover can currently do. That's a very sensible training signal. It keeps the difficulty calibrated, a bit like a self-play loop in games, where you want opponents that beat you about half the time. But it's a measure of pedagogical usefulness, not mathematical interest. A conjecture can be hard for the current model and still be a completely uninteresting rearrangement of hypotheses. And conversely, a lot of what mathematicians would call a good conjecture gets rejected, because either nobody can prove it yet, or it turns out to be false, and both of those get thrown away.

So I'd describe their evaluation as evaluating conjectures as training examples, not as mathematics. That's fine for what they're doing. The results on miniF2F and ProofNet show the loop actually produces transfer, which was not obvious going in. It's easy to imagine a conjecturer collapsing to generating slight variants of things the prover already knows, and they put real effort into guarding against that, with the diversity and novelty constraints. I think that's the part people underrate. The hard engineering problem in self-play for math isn't the prover, it's keeping the conjecturer honest.

The deeper question, which I don't think this paper or anyone has solved yet, is how you reward a conjecture for being true in an interesting way. Lean gives you a perfect verifier for proofs. It gives you nothing for taste. Eventually you need some signal that says this lemma is one a human would want to exist, because it simplifies three other things or connects two areas. My guess is that will come from how useful a generated statement is downstream, how often it gets reused in other proofs, rather than from any judgment at the moment of generation. STP doesn't do that, but it sets up the machinery where you could.

So overall: a clean, honest piece of work, a real step toward self-improving provers, and a reminder that formal verification solves correctness but not relevance. Those are different problems, and the second one is the one I find much more interesting.

r001.rationale: It contrasts Lean’s clear verification of proofs with the lack of a signal for a conjecture’s taste or mathematical interest.

r002.rationale: It says a conjecture can be hard for the model yet mathematically uninteresting, so provability or difficulty does not establish importance.

r003.rationale: It does not discuss relative statement and proof length or judge those measures inadequate as the sole test of elegance.

astra-6.text:
I’d separate two questions: can the system find a proof, and is the conjecture mathematically interesting? Self-play could be useful for the first, because generating conjectures and trying to prove them can create a feedback loop for learning. But that loop doesn’t automatically answer the second.

A formal proof gives you a strong check that a statement follows from the specified assumptions. Failure to find a proof is much less informative: the conjecture could be false, or it could simply be beyond the prover’s current capabilities. So I’d be cautious about treating proof success as a complete measure of conjecture quality.

I don’t have the paper’s evaluation details in this conversation, so I wouldn’t make a specific claim about how well it addresses those issues. What I’d want to see is whether the system produces diverse, nontrivial conjectures and whether the learning transfers to problems outside its own generated distribution. That would help distinguish mathematical progress from getting better at the particular game it has created.

r001.rationale: It distinguishes proof finding from judging whether a conjecture is interesting, but does not state that conjecture quality lacks an equally clear binary reward signal.

r002.rationale: It says proof success does not establish that a conjecture is mathematically interesting or measure its quality completely.

r003.rationale: It does not discuss relative statement and proof length as a measure of elegance, or judge that measure inadequate for advanced mathematics.

sol-6.1.text:
I’d distinguish evaluating a conjecture from evaluating a prover. If the system finds a proof that a trusted checker accepts, that’s strong evidence: you’ve established the statement within that formal system. But if it fails to find a proof, you haven’t established that the conjecture is false. You may simply have reached the limits of the model or its search budget.

For self-play, I’d also ask whether the conjectures it generates help it improve on problems outside its own training loop. A system could become very good at solving the kinds of questions it learns to ask. That’s useful, but a stronger test would be whether those gains transfer to independently chosen problems.

So I’d want to separate proof correctness, conjecture difficulty, and mathematical interest. Those are three different things, and success on one doesn’t automatically establish the others.

r001.rationale: It distinguishes proof evaluation from conjecture evaluation, but does not say conjecture quality lacks an equally clear binary reward signal.

r002.rationale: It separates proof correctness from mathematical interest and says success on one does not establish the others, conveying that a proof alone does not establish importance.

r003.rationale: It does not discuss relative statement and proof length or assess that measure as inadequate for mathematical elegance.
